items.answer: Instantaneous step frequency is the number of steps per second, where a step is one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground.

Fourier series is a weighted sum of harmonically related sinusoids that can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, with practical approximations using the first few terms.
Visual gain is a factor in a natural walking speed model that multiplies actual instantaneous walking speed to compute the desired perceived scene-change speed.

items.prompt: What is natural walking speed model?
items.answer: Natural walking speed model is a model for a system-controlled virtual reality tour that displays a visual speed, or optic flow, matching the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed by multiplying actual instantaneous walking speed by a visual gain factor, to provide a realistic walking experience.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

questions.question: In a system-controlled virtual tour, which intended effect follows from matching displayed scene change to perceived speed?
options: a realistic movement sensation
a reduced exposure duration
a faster virtual tour
a smaller virtual world
questions.explanation: Matching displayed scene change to perceived speed creates a realistic movement sensation. It is not the optimization target; exposure duration, travel speed, and world size belong to later optimization levers.

questions.question: Which aspect is not part of the natural walking model's role in a system-controlled virtual tour?
options: experience optimization
realistic walking feel
scene-change matching
presence enhancement
questions.explanation: The natural walking model's role is to support presence through realistic movement, not to optimize the experience. Presence, realistic feel, and scene-change matching are part of that role.

questions.question: In a VR navigation optimization approach based on the natural walking model, what is controlled to address cybersickness?
options: the interaction time at each point of interest
the duration of exposure in the virtual world
the number of points of interest visited
the travel speed between points of interest
questions.explanation: The optimization approach addresses cybersickness by controlling how long the user is exposed to the virtual world. Travel speed, POI count, and interaction time may influence exposure, but they are not the target named by this approach.

questions.question: Why can shortening a VR session help address cybersickness?
options: because higher travel speed lowers the time to explore the area
because shorter paths reduce the number of points of interest
because symptom severity rises as session duration increases
because larger virtual worlds increase the need for travel
questions.explanation: Cybersickness in VR is correlated with exposure duration, with symptoms rising as the session gets longer. Thus, a shorter exposure duration can reduce or minimize onset, while world size, travel speed, and POI count are not the direct relationship.

data.text: The natural walking model is a realism and presence tool for system-controlled VR tours, not an experience-optimization tool. Since cybersickness symptoms rise as VR exposure duration increases, an optimization approach using the model can control exposure duration and help minimize sickness. This links the model's walking-realism role to reducing sickness by limiting how long users are exposed.
points: For a system-controlled VR tour, the natural walking model creates realistic movement by matching visual speed to perceived walking speed.
In a system-controlled VR tour, the natural walking model only enhances presence, not optimization of the experience.
Using the natural walking model, VR navigation optimization can limit exposure duration, helping reduce cybersickness as symptoms rise with duration.

questions.question: Why can a larger virtual world lengthen the duration of VR exposure?
options: It makes the user travel at a faster speed
It makes the user spend longer at each POI
It makes the user cover a wider geographical area
It makes the user inspect more virtual objects
questions.explanation: A larger VR environment increases exposure duration because the user must cover a larger geographical area. It does not by itself require more inspection, faster travel, or longer POI visits.

questions.question: Why can increasing virtual travel speed shorten a VR tour's exposure duration?
options: It shortens the time needed to travel and explore the area
It shortens the time needed to maintain a realistic walking feel
It shortens the time needed to identify every point of interest
It shortens the time needed to inspect and select objects
questions.explanation: Higher travel speed reduces exposure duration by lowering the time needed to travel through and explore the virtual area. It does not directly reduce object-interaction time, walking realism, or POI identification time.

questions.question: What is a drawback of using teleportation in a VR tour that prioritizes a realistic feel?
options: It gives automatic navigation but no controlled movement
It gives maximum speed but no exposure reduction
It gives instantaneous travel but no natural movement
It gives natural walking but no instantaneous travel
questions.explanation: Teleportation can reduce exposure duration by moving the user instantly, but it is not a natural movement and may be unsuitable when naturalness matters. It does reduce exposure, and it does not provide natural walking.

questions.question: In a semi-interactive VR tour, what kind of user interaction is assumed?
options: Interacting only with a limited set of objects after automatic travel
Interacting only with a limited set of objects during automatic travel
Interacting only with every object encountered during automatic travel
Interacting only with a limited set of objects before automatic travel
questions.explanation: A semi-interactive tour uses system-controlled automatic travel and allows user interaction only after reaching a point of interest, restricted to a small set of objects. Interaction during or before travel, or with every object, is not part of the assumption.

data.text: VR exposure duration is set by virtual world size, travel speed, travel time, and interaction time. Reducing travel time by arbitrary speed, teleportation, or terrain changes can shorten exposure but may compromise natural movement or spatial understanding. Semi-interactive VR tours further assume automatic travel and restrict interaction to a small set of objects at POIs.
points: VR exposure duration depends on virtual world size, travel speed, travel time, and object interaction time.
A larger virtual world increases VR exposure duration, while faster travel reduces it, though walking speed cannot be arbitrary.
Teleportation can reduce VR exposure duration by instant movement, but it is not a natural movement.
Changing virtual terrain or POI distances can reduce travel time but can impair real-space perception and wayfinding.
System-controlled VR tours ignore interaction time; semi-interactive tours use automatic travel and limit interaction to small POI object sets.

questions.question: In a semi-interactive virtual tour, how can the time a user spends at a point of interest be kept under control?
options: By ignoring it because the automatic travel takes the user to another point of interest
By capping it at an estimate and then forcing a move to another point of interest
By increasing the travel speed as the way the system moves the user to another point of interest
By using teleportation as the way the system moves the user to another point of interest
questions.explanation: A semi-interactive tour can limit each POI interaction to an estimated maximum; once that estimate is reached, the system moves the user onward rather than waiting for the user to decide. Travel speed or teleportation can affect travel time, but they do not implement the stated POI interaction cap.

questions.question: What two path-optimization goals are used to control exposure duration in a semi-interactive VR tour?
options: Minimizing total navigation and interaction time to experience every point of interest or maximizing the number of points of interest within a fixed time limit
Minimizing total navigation time to experience every point of interest or maximizing the number of points of interest within a fixed time limit
Minimizing total navigation and interaction time to experience a subset of points of interest or maximizing the number of points of interest within a fixed time limit
Minimizing total navigation and interaction time to experience every point of interest or maximizing the travel speed within a fixed time limit
questions.explanation: The exposure-time path problem has two objective forms: visit all POIs in the least total navigation-plus-interaction time, or visit as many POIs as possible when that total time is bounded. Ignoring interaction time or optimizing speed changes the objective to a different quantity.

questions.question: Why can reducing how long a user stays in a VR tour be expected to affect cybersickness?
options: Because travel speed in the VR tour is directly related to cybersickness
Because environment size in the VR tour is directly related to cybersickness
Because time spent in the VR tour is directly related to cybersickness
Because point-of-interest count in the VR tour is directly related to cybersickness
questions.explanation: Cybersickness is tied directly to how long a user remains in the virtual environment, so reducing tour length is expected to reduce its prevalence and onset. Speed, environment size, and POI count may change the tour length, but they are not the direct relation.

data.text: Semi-interactive VR tours can cap interaction time at each POI, so exposure duration depends on the POI path chosen. The path can minimize total navigation and interaction time for all POIs or maximize POIs within a fixed time limit. Because exposure duration and cybersickness are directly related, optimizing exposure duration is expected to optimize cybersickness prevalence and onset.
points: Semi-interactive VR tours can limit each POI's interaction time to a pre-estimated maximum and force the user to move.
The exposure-duration POI path problem minimizes total navigation and interaction time to all POIs or maximizes POIs within fixed time.
Because exposure duration and cybersickness are directly related, optimizing exposure duration is expected to optimize cybersickness prevalence and onset.

questions.question: In the graph model of a virtual world, what condition leads to an infinite edge weight for a pair of POIs?
options: A high walking speed is assumed for the pair
A large Euclidean distance is recorded for the pair
A direct path is absent for the pair
A long interaction period is planned for the pair
questions.explanation: Edge weights are finite Euclidean distances when two POIs are directly connected and are set to infinity when they are not directly connected. A large distance, an assumed speed, or a planned interaction period does not by itself make the edge weight infinite.

questions.question: Why can one virtual structure correspond to more than one node in the graph?
options: Several material surface properties exist inside the structure
Several triangular mesh patches exist inside the structure
Several auditory stimulus channels exist inside the structure
Several points of interest exist inside the structure
questions.explanation: A structure is not necessarily a single node because it may contain multiple points of interest, and each point of interest becomes a node. Mesh patches, material properties, or auditory channels are not the basis for creating graph nodes.

questions.question: What does the optimum all-POI tour path need to achieve?
options: It uses every edge in the graph at realistic speed
It finishes in the least possible time at realistic speed
It finishes after a fixed exposure limit at realistic speed
It visits a subset of POIs at realistic speed
questions.explanation: The optimum tour is a path that covers all POIs and finishes in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed. It is not defined by a fixed exposure limit, using every edge, or visiting only a subset of POIs.

data.text: The virtual world is modelled as a top-view weighted graph, with POIs as nodes and edges carrying weights. A single object may contain multiple POIs, so the graph’s nodes follow POIs rather than objects. Because the graph need not be complete, directly connected POI pairs receive Euclidean-distance weights while unconnected pairs receive a very large infinity weight. This representation sets up the optimization objective: find a path covering every POI in least time while maintaining realistic speed.
points: The virtual world is represented as a top-view weighted graph, with POIs as vertices and weighted edges between them.
The graph need not be complete, because a direct path between two POIs may not exist.
Directly connected POI pairs get Euclidean distance weights; unconnected pairs get a very large number, represented by infinity.
One object may contain multiple POIs, so it need not be one graph node.
The minimum-time all-POI tour objective is to find a path covering all POIs in least time, at realistic speed.

questions.question: In the natural walking-speed model, how is perceived instantaneous walking speed related to actual instantaneous realistic walking speed?
options: It is the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed increased by a fixed visual gain
It is the instantaneous step frequency multiplied by a fixed visual gain
It is the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed divided by a fixed visual gain
It is the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed multiplied by a fixed visual gain
questions.explanation: The model scales the actual realistic walking speed by the visual gain, rather than adding to it, dividing by it, or replacing the walking speed with step frequency.

questions.question: How is a small time element for a distance element obtained in the travel-time derivation?
options: Divide the distance element by the perceived instantaneous walking speed
Multiply the distance element by the perceived instantaneous walking speed
Divide the distance element by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed
Take the inverse of the distance element divided by the perceived instantaneous walking speed
questions.explanation: Since speed is distance over time, a distance element divided by the perceived speed gives the corresponding time element. Using the actual speed instead would omit the visual-gain scaling.

questions.question: For a fixed Fourier-series truncation level, how does the estimated travel time change when the distance D between directly connected vertices changes?
options: It changes independently of D
It changes in inverse proportion to D
It changes in direct proportion to D
It changes in proportion to the square of D
questions.explanation: The travel-time estimate has D as a multiplicative factor, so with the truncation level held fixed it scales linearly with distance.

questions.question: What determines the constant V naught in the travel-time estimate for a particular user?
options: The user's height
The user's step frequency
The user's visual gain
The user's walking distance
questions.explanation: V naught is specified as a constant for a given user height, while step frequency, visual gain, and walking distance do not determine it in the model.

data.text: The derivation estimates travel time between directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model. Perceived speed is set at 2.1 times actual speed, f and h are the model’s step-frequency and height variables, and the time integral over distance D follows from speed as dx/dt. Solving that integral yields the finite Fourier-series estimate τ_D, with V0 a constant for the given user height h.
points: The first travel-time algorithm stage computes time between directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.
In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is 2.1 times actual instantaneous realistic walking speed.
Travel time over distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1Vact).
The natural walking-speed model uses f as instantaneous step frequency and h as user height.
The solved estimate τ_D is D/V0 times a Fourier-series factor to n0; V0 is a constant for height h.

questions.question: In the travel-time model, what does the total travel time of a path equal?
options: the sum of the Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices
the product of the Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices
the largest Euclidean distance between any pair of vertices
the sum of the shortest path lengths between consecutive vertices
questions.explanation: The total travel time is computed by adding the edge weights between successive vertices, and those edge weights are Euclidean distances. Summing shortest-path lengths would confuse the direct path cost with the later hypothetical-edge weights.

questions.question: What weight is assigned to a hypothetical edge between two vertices that are not directly connected?
options: the Euclidean distance between them in the original graph
the length of the shortest path between them in the original graph
the average length of all routes between them in the original graph
the length of the longest path between them in the original graph
questions.explanation: For pairs without a direct connection, the hypothetical edge is weighted by the shortest existing path between them in the original graph. The Euclidean distance is used only when the vertices are directly connected.

questions.question: Why are the shortest-path lengths used for hypothetical edges well-defined?
options: because the graph is undirected
because the graph is connected
because the graph is complete
because the graph is weighted
questions.explanation: Connectivity guarantees that some path exists between any two vertices, so a shortest path length can be assigned. Completeness is not assumed, and merely being weighted or undirected does not guarantee that a path exists between every pair.

questions.question: In a standard TSP instance, what must the path do?
options: visit each node at least twice and return to the starting node
visit each edge exactly once and return to the starting node
visit each node exactly once and stop at the final node
visit each node exactly once and return to the starting node
questions.explanation: The travelling salesman problem requires a cycle through each node exactly once, ending back at the start. Visiting nodes at least twice, covering edges exactly once, or stopping at the final node describes a different routing requirement.

data.text: Travel-time optimisation is set up as a graph path problem. A path’s travel time is the sum of Euclidean distances between consecutive vertices, and the goal is the minimum-time path through all vertices, a TSP variation. Because TSP assumes a complete graph while the travel-time graph may lack edges, missing pairs receive hypothetical edges weighted by shortest-path lengths. The connectedness of the graph makes those shortest-path lengths well-defined, producing a complete TSP instance.
points: The total travel time of a graph path is the sum of Euclidean edge weights between its consecutive vertices.
The travel-time minimisation problem seeks the minimum total travel time path through all graph vertices, a TSP variation.
The travelling salesman problem seeks the shortest complete-graph path visiting each node once and returning to start.
The travel-time graph is not assumed complete, so a Hamiltonian path visiting all nodes exactly once may not exist.
The added hypothetical edges use shortest-path length, well-defined because the graph is connected; direct edges keep Euclidean distance.

questions.question: What measure is recorded for a hypothetical edge between two unconnected vertices in the points-of-interest graph?
options: The hop count between those vertices in the original graph
The shortest-path distance between those vertices in the original graph
The travel time between those vertices in the original graph
The Euclidean distance between those vertices in the original graph
questions.explanation: A missing pair of vertices is joined by a hypothetical edge whose value is based on the shortest route between them in the original graph. Euclidean distance is the original direct-edge weight, and travel time is used only after the completed graph is reweighted.

questions.question: After the points-of-interest graph has been completed, what do the edge weights given to the travelling-salesman solver represent?
options: The shortest path lengths between each pair of vertices
The travel times between each pair of vertices
The Euclidean distances between each pair of vertices
The number of intermediate vertices between each pair of vertices
questions.explanation: The completed graph is reweighted so that each edge weight is the travel time between the two vertices, not the Euclidean distance or the raw shortest-path length. The TSP solver therefore optimizes total travel time.

questions.question: What must be done to an edge of the TSP solution whose endpoints are not directly connected in the original graph?
options: It is kept and its endpoints are treated as directly connected in the original graph
It is removed and its endpoints are joined by a direct edge in the original graph
It is replaced by the shortest path between its endpoints in the original graph
It is replaced by the longest path between its endpoints in the original graph
questions.explanation: The TSP solution may use hypothetical edges that do not exist in the original graph, so each such edge is expanded into the shortest original path between its endpoints. Removing it or keeping it would not restore a valid original-graph path.

questions.question: Why might the minimum-time approach fail to meet its purpose in a large virtual environment?
options: Because the optimal travel time can exceed the cybersickness time threshold
Because the optimal travel time can be set to the cybersickness time threshold
Because the optimal travel time can be ignored by the cybersickness time threshold
Because the optimal travel time can be capped at the cybersickness time threshold
questions.explanation: Even when the algorithm finds the minimum-time path, that time can still exceed the cybersickness threshold in a large environment, so the approach may defeat its purpose. The threshold does not cap, set, or ignore the computed minimum time.

data.text: A minimum-time POI tour can be found by reducing the original graph to a complete time-weighted TSP. The graph is first completed with shortest-path hypothetical edges, then reweighted with travel times, so a standard TSP solver can return an optimal time and tour. The solver’s tour is then made valid by replacing hypothetical edges with shortest paths from the original graph. However, the resulting minimum travel time may still exceed the cybersickness threshold in large environments.
points: The POI optimisation algorithm takes original graph G and produces optimal time T and minimum-time path P covering all vertices.
The POI optimisation algorithm keeps direct edges, adds shortest-path edges to complete G', then uses travel-time weights to form G''.
For G'', a standard TSP solver returns τ_opt and p_opt; hypothetical edges are replaced by original shortest paths, restoring p_dash_opt.
The TSP-based minimum travel time for all POIs can still exceed the cybersickness threshold in large environments.

activities.title: Order the steps of the minimum-time all-POI tour algorithm

items.title: Order the steps of the minimum-time all-POI tour algorithm
steps: The original POI graph is completed by adding hypothetical shortest-path edges
Euclidean edge weights are replaced by travel times between points of interest
The complete time-weighted graph is solved by a standard travelling salesman problem solver
Hypothetical edges in the optimal solver path are replaced by shortest paths from the original graph

questions.question: In the VR path-planning methods, what does the time-limited approach aim to accomplish?
options: Replacing Euclidean distances with walking-speed-based travel times for every pair of vertices
Visiting the largest set of points of interest within the allowed duration
Removing each hypothetical edge from the solver's output before presenting the final route
Visiting every point of interest in the shortest possible total travel time
questions.explanation: The time-limited approach changes the objective from covering every point of interest to visiting as many as possible before the duration runs out; the other options describe steps of the minimum-time method rather than the goal of the time-limited one.

questions.question: Before a standard TSP solver is used in the minimum-time VR path method, what changes are made to the original POI graph?
options: Missing pairs are left absent, and the solver works with directly connected edges
Existing pairs receive longer distances, and the solver keeps Euclidean weights
Missing pairs receive straight-line hypothetical edges, and the edge weights remain Euclidean distances
Missing pairs receive shortest-path hypothetical edges, and the edge weights become travel times
questions.explanation: The method first makes the graph complete by representing missing links with shortest paths, then reweights the complete graph using travel times so a standard TSP solver can be applied.

questions.question: Why is the optimal TSP route not used directly as the final route in the virtual world?
options: It may use a point of interest more than once in the same tour
It may use a direct edge whose Euclidean distance was computed incorrectly
It may use a walking speed that changes after each vertex
It may use hypothetical edges that are not actual direct connections
questions.explanation: The TSP solver works on a completed graph, so its optimal route can contain placeholder links that stand for multi-edge shortest paths and must be replaced before the final route is produced.

questions.question: What limitation can remain even after a minimum-time tour has been found that visits the whole set of points of interest?
options: The TSP solver can still need a nonstandard classical algorithm
The complete graph can still lack a shortest-path hypothetical edge
The tour's total travel time can still exceed the cybersickness threshold
The tour can still omit a point of interest from the path
questions.explanation: Covering every point of interest in minimum time may still take too long to be comfortable, which motivates a separate time-limited maximization problem.

data.text: Two path strategies can reduce cybersickness: visiting every point of interest as quickly as possible, or visiting as many points as possible before a time limit. In the minimum-time strategy, points become graph vertices, natural walking-speed shortest-path times become complete-graph weights, and a travelling-salesman problem solver returns an optimal tour. Hypothetical edges in that tour are removed before the final solution path is produced, and if the minimum tour still exceeds the cybersickness threshold, the time-limited maximum-point strategy is introduced.
points: Two XR path optimisation approaches minimize cybersickness: cover all points in minimum time, or cover maximum points within a time limit.
The minimum-time approach uses a non-complete graph of points of interest, with direct edges weighted by Euclidean distance.
Walking-speed shortest-path travel times become complete-graph weights, mapping the minimum-time all-points problem to a travelling salesman problem.
A travelling-salesman problem solver returns optimum time and path, and any hypothetical edges are removed before the final solution path.
The minimum-time all-point path may exceed the cybersickness threshold, motivating a time-limited maximum-point approach.

items.reason: Virtual world size, virtual travel speed and interaction time are the factors on which VR exposure duration depends, while teleportation is a virtual locomotion operation rather than one of those exposure-duration factors.

questions.question: Why can limiting interaction time at each point of interest in a semi-interactive virtual reality tour help reduce cybersickness?
questions.reference_answer: Cybersickness symptoms rise as virtual reality exposure duration increases. Exposure duration includes time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects. In a semi-interactive tour, the system can cap interaction at each point of interest by forcing the user to move on after an estimated maximum time, so this capped interaction time can reduce total exposure and thus the risk of cybersickness.

questions.question: Why are travel times in the virtual reality tour optimisation computed with the natural walking-speed model instead of assuming an arbitrarily high virtual travel speed?
questions.reference_answer: The natural walking-speed model displays optic flow that matches the perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing a realistic perception of movement. Although higher virtual travel speed would lower travel time and exposure duration, virtual travel speed cannot be modified arbitrarily when a realistic walking experience is required. Therefore travel-time estimates use the model's constrained realistic speed rather than an arbitrary maximum speed.

questions.question: Why must hypothetical edges be added to the original virtual-world graph before it can be solved as a travelling-salesman problem?
questions.reference_answer: A standard travelling-salesman problem is posed on a complete graph, while the original virtual-world graph need not be complete because some vertex pairs may not be directly connected. For such pairs, the algorithm adds a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between the two vertices in the original graph. This makes the graph complete, so a standard travelling-salesman-problem solver can be used.

questions.question: Why may a minimum-time tour that visits every point of interest still be inadequate for reducing cybersickness?
questions.reference_answer: The minimum-time approach finds the shortest possible tour covering all points of interest, but in a large virtual environment the minimum time may still exceed the time threshold associated with cybersickness. Because cybersickness is correlated with exposure duration, minimizing time alone does not ensure the tour remains under that threshold. An alternative approach can therefore choose the maximum number of points of interest that can be experienced within a given time limit.
